en: The Subhūtyavadāna, the tenth in the Garland of Avadānas of the Kalpadruma.
Then King Aśoka, with all his sorrows dispelled,
bowed to his teacher Upagupta and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear yet another well-spoken word;
you should tell me that which was spoken by the Lion of the Śākyas."
Thus questioned by the king, Upagupta, the lord of ascetics,
surveyed the assembly and spoke these well-spoken words:
Listen, O King of mighty arms, for the sake of the welfare of all the world,
to the legend of Subhūti which I shall proclaim just as I have heard it.
In the past, the Blessed One, the Buddha, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata,
was perfected in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the Conqueror of the world.
The Teacher of gods and humans, the expounder of perfect enlightenment,
is honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by sentient beings.
By kings and royal ministers, by wealthy city-dwellers, by guild-leaders and caravan-merchants gathered from various lands; KDA_7 //
By the great gods and asuras, by the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras,
by the garuḍas and great serpents, and likewise by other species of sentient beings.
Well-restrained and possessing great merit, he was a recipient of robes and garments,
as well as alms-food, seats, and likewise bedding and other requisites.
May there always be, in every respect, provisions such as medicines and other requisites for the Saṅgha together with their disciples, and for the monks who have conquered their senses.
And likewise by bhikṣuṇīs and upāsikās, by celakas and upāsakas,
and by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who desire awakening for the sake of sentient beings.
In the royal capital of Śrāvastī, at the delightful Jetavana monastery,
he dwelt constantly teaching the Dharma that leads to auspiciousness.
Then, desiring to discipline and favor sentient beings, the Blessed One addressed all the monks and gave them this correct instruction: // KDA_13 //
"Go forth, O monks, for the sake of disciplining sentient beings; traveling through various lands, proclaim the way of righteousness."
Having promised "So be it," and having bowed at the feet of the Teacher, those disciples and monks who were appointed set forth. (KDA 15)
Carrying out the command of their Guru, some of them went to the eastern direction and, establishing themselves in various regions, they taught the True Dharma.
Likewise, some went to the southern direction, some to the western direction,
and others to the northern direction, as well as everywhere toward the intermediate directions.
Those who were indeed devoted to meditation, seeking the bliss of solitude and intent on dhyāna, dwelt upon the upper terraces of Mount Meru.
Then, a single young serpent was pulled from the ocean by Garuḍa;
having brought it to that hermitage, he proceeded to devour it.
Seeing those monks dwelling there, absorbed in meditation, that nāga, with a very serene mind, made this aspiration: KDA_20.
Blessed indeed are those monks who dwell happily in the true Dharma;
may I too become one thus absorbed in the Dharma.
While making this vow,
that nāga was deprived of life and was devoured right there by the garuḍa in this manner.
Then, having passed away there in the city of Śrāvastī,
he entered the womb of the wife of a brahmin named Bhūti.
Thereupon, her pregnancy gradually increased,
and when the time had arrived, a boy was born.
Then his father, seeing that boy who was so inspiring, handsome,
and possessed of such beautiful limbs, gazed upon him again and again, O Ānanda.
Then, having performed the birth festival, he respectfully summoned the wise men and said, "Sirs, what name should be given to him? (KDA 26)
Having heard this and having seen that boy, his kinsmen were all filled with joy and spoke thus to Bhūti: KDA_27.
"Since this well-born son endowed with auspicious marks has come from Bhūti,
let him therefore be known by the name Subhūti."
Thus, having gradually grown up, that Subhūti, beautiful as a youth,
attained the state of boyhood in due course and enjoyed himself, endowed with his youth.
Due to the reinforcement of the power of his past karma, he became irascible and harsh in speech; provoked by even a slight cause, he became intent on conflict. (KDA 30)
Because his mind had become harsh, no one was his friend;
because he was at odds with all his kinsmen, he was even neglected by his parents.
Abandoned by his kinsmen and no longer dear to anyone,
no one spoke to him with confidence or affection.
No one at all dared to stand, walk, eat, lie down, or even speak in the presence of that wrathful one.
Then, commissioned by his father, he went to the school;
and Subhūti, having bowed to his teacher, mastered writing in due order.
Then, having studied all the sciences in due order, beginning with grammar,
that highly intelligent one very swiftly reached their further shore.
Having thus studied the Vedas, along with their limbs and sub-limbs, in due order, he,
being of sharp intellect, then began to study the Atharva Veda as well.
There, the father, the twice-born Bhūti, having seen his own son Subhūti, who was fully devoted to the study of the Atharva Veda, reflected thus: (KDA 37)
"This Subhūti is my son, like fire, with an exceedingly sharp intellect; if he should ever become angry, out of his wrath he will bring about misfortune in the world. (KDA 38)
"Therefore, this [text] must be retrieved with effort from the Atharvaṇa;
having sent him among the sages, I shall employ him for the purpose of restraint. (KDA 39)
Thinking thus, the father Bhūti, having extracted his own son Subhūti from the Atharva Veda, spoke to him while awakening him: KDA 40.
Listen, my son, to what I have spoken for your benefit and with your welfare in mind;
for you are learned, possessed of great wisdom, and have mastered all the scriptures and their auxiliary branches.
What use have you for the Atharvaveda, which accomplishes only magical illusions and worldly aims?
Desist from that foundation and practice the conduct of a sage.
Having received the instructions of the sages, with senses conquered and mind tranquil, abide in happiness and practice the supreme vow.
Blessed are those free from passion who are devoted to their guru and devoid of pride,
who dwell in secluded forest retreats, always absorbed in meditation.
Even those who, having renounced possessions, become practitioners of celibacy,
are indeed always worthy of honor and salutation even by the gods. (KDA 45)
Those who, having embraced the life of renunciation, dwell with peaceful minds and conquered senses in sacred pilgrimage sites— they too are indeed supreme seers.
Those best of the twice-born who, having abandoned objects of sensual enjoyment, practice their discipline in the forest of penance, content with fruits, roots, and water— they too are blessed.
Even those who, having conquered the afflictions, dwell in the four divine abodes,
subsist on alms, and abide in meditative concentration— they indeed are the foremost among the knowers of Brahman.
Those who possess nothing, who are free from greed, speakers of truth,
devoid of pride and free from egoism— they alone are the supreme brahmins.
For one whose mind is overcome by stinginess and who has no desire to give, what is the use of the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Agamas? Such a person is merely nourishing his own self.
For one whose mind is indeed impure and who is devoid of the restraint of ethical discipline, what is the use of the garb of a sage? He is like a mad actor-sage.
For one who has no compassion in this world for those suffering— such as children, the elderly, and others—
what is the use of the conduct of a Brahmin when their mind is utterly deluded?
For one whose mind lacks the zeal to accomplish the welfare of the world through wholesome means, what is the use of asceticism? It is achieved solely through causes of evil.
One whose mind is distracted by afflictions and remains unconcentrated—
how can such a person not be wicked, even if dwelling in a cave, like a malevolent beast?
For one whose wisdom is not purified in the accomplishment of the qualities of the True Dharma,
what is the use of celibacy, which is merely a cause of suffering?
And whoever is a donor, pure in soul and a protector of all beings—
even if lowly— he is like a twice-born, because the donor is Prajāpati.
He whose ethical conduct is constantly protected, restrained, and governed—
only he is a pure brahmin, a learned scholar, and an ascetic who has mastered the Vedas.
He whose mind has compassion as its spear and who strives for the welfare of all beings—even if he be an outcaste, he would be a brahmin; for he is a lord of the world, a maker of patience.
He by whom difficult deeds were accomplished for the sake of sentient beings—
he alone is the wise Brāhmaṇa, Viśvakarman, from whom the ritual procedure originates.

He whose mind is always concentrated on the welfare of sentient beings is indeed a Brahmin possessing great higher knowledge (*mahābhijñā*), for he is one who delights in Brahma-like wisdom (*jñāna*).
Delighting in meditative concentration. // KDA_60 //
He whose wisdom shines forth as an instruction for the welfare of the world is the best of the twice-born; he alone is the wise brahmin who stands firm in the dharma of the Vedas.
He by whom the afflictions have been utterly conquered through the four divine abodes,
and who has cultivated the sublime within his own mind— he alone is the supreme brahmin.
Therefore, my son, having heard what I have spoken, be eager for the welfare of the world;
having completely conquered all afflictions, be devoted to the true Dharma.
Having heard these words of his father, Subhūti rejoiced;
bowing with palms joined, he addressed his father thus: (KDA 64)
"Since, dear father, my mind finds truth pleasing for the sake of asceticism, therefore grant me your permission, father; I shall practice the excellent vow of Brahman."
Thus entreated by Subhūti, his father then embraced his son and spoke once more with joy: KDA_66: "Thus entreated by Subhūti, his father then embraced his son and spoke once more with joy."
If you have such a desire, my son, through the excellent means of Brahman,
practice the vow of Brahman properly, with a firm mind and concentrated composure.
First, having conquered the enemy that is anger, you must utterly defeat the wicked burdens;
for as long as you have not conquered anger, you will not be able to conquer the wicked.
As long as you have not conquered the wicked, you will not be able to abide in the Dharma;
for Māras will surely destroy one whose Dharma is not well-established in every way.
Therefore, he who desires Brahman must first extract from the hollow of his mind the serpent of anger and slay it with diligent effort.
For as long as anger dwells in one's mind, agitated by pride and intoxication,
that person is not served by the virtuous, even if they are endowed with excellent qualities.
Therefore, with every effort, being concentrated and victorious over anger,
rely upon the life of renunciation and practice the state of a Brahmin with devotion.
Having promised "So be it," Subhūti, filled with joy,
bowed suddenly to his parents and went to the hermitage of the sages.
Having arrived there and bowed to the sages with palms joined in reverence,
he joyfully requested ordination in order to receive the vows of a brahmin.
O Guru, best among the knowers of Brahman, guide on the path to welfare! Grant me the going-forth; may I truly practice for the sake of liberation from cyclic existence. (KDA 75)
Having heard these words of his, the Guru, the best among the knowers of Brahman, said: "Come, my child; practice the life of a student of sacred knowledge, having conquered the six senses."
Thus addressed by the Guru, Subhūti, wearing the garb of a sage, became perfected in the divine abodes,
disciplined, and endowed with faith.
Nevertheless, by the power of fate, his mind colored by anger,
even at the slightest pretext, he became uncontrolled and engaged in conflict.
A disputant regarding the Vedas, established doctrines, and scriptures, abounding in anger and excessively tormented by rage, even insulted the ascetics.
Indifferent toward virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, and possessing exceedingly harsh speech,
he was everywhere refuted by the sages as being lacking in composure.
Seeing the brahmin Subhūti thus flushed with anger and proud of his mastery of the Vedic tenets, his teacher reflected as follows.
Ah! By the power of fate, even this Brahmin Subhūti today, like one of our own school, is eager for a debate using harsh words. (KDA 82)
Resembling fire, exceedingly sharp, and skilled in the meaning of all scriptures;
confident, highly wise, and devoted to the restraint of the Dharma.
Devoted to the practice of austerity, sharp-witted, and diligent in his efforts,
he was one of great energy, a great hero, accomplished in the sciences, and exceedingly formidable.
He was a master of all scriptures and arts, an expert in the application of mantra-siddhi,
a great sage who had reached the further shore of the Vedas, Siddhāntas, and Yoga.
However, one whose self is unpurified by anger, who is contentious and addicted to debate, becomes provoked even by a mere pretext, with a mind full of resentment. (KDA 86)
At times, when provoked and enraged, his mind unsteady due to afflictions,
he will bring misfortune upon the world with the stroke of a thunderbolt of a curse.
Therefore, having fully awakened this Subhūti, the best of the twice-born,
I shall by all means engage him in the most excellent meditative absorptions and concentrations.
Thinking thus, the Guru enlightened Subhūti:
"Listen, my child; I shall speak what is beneficial. Be attentive to it."
The Brahmin is the first-born of all castes and the highest among all classes;
yet, one should never harbor the egoistic conceit, "I am a Brahmin. (KDA 90)
The living soul (*jīva*) is not a Brahmin, because one becomes twice-born (*dvija*) through ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*);
if the living soul were already a Brahmin, then the ritual refinements of dharma would be in vain.
It is stated even in the Veda that "at the beginning and at the end [of creation] there are animals and gods";
therefore, through the performance of dharma, all human beings may become twice-born (dvijas).

Even outcastes (śvapacas) may become established in dharma and refined, while the lowest of the twice-born (dvijādhamas) may fall; likewise, gods, demons, and humans arise according to their qualities and the performance of dharma.

"The gods are bearers of the quality of goodness (sattva), humans are bearers of the quality of passion (rajas), and the Daityas are bearers of the quality of darkness (tamas); such is the established doctrine."
Thus, due to the implantation of the qualities of phenomena within the abode of existence in the three realms,
those born from the four modes of birth wander through the six destinies.
Even there, indeed, there are numerous distinctions of birth according to the distinction of karma;
and within all those births as well, [distinctions arise] through the transformation of one's own karma.
Sentient beings are born of many kinds— inferior, superior, and middling.
Those beings who are characterized by darkness (*tamas*), who are fierce, and who are devoted to acts of violence,
are born in the lower worlds and dwell there as partakers of affliction.
Those beings who delight in the nature of passion and follow the conduct of attachment are born on the earth and dwell as humans and other such creatures.
But those who delight in the dharma of sentient beings, who are sattvic and peaceful in conduct,
having gone to the celestial realm, dwell there as gods with stainless bliss.
In the same way, all these sentient beings, following after qualities and dharmas,
wander through the abode of the three realms of existence while experiencing the results of their own actions.
In this manner, the qualities increase one by one through the augmentation of qualities:
space has only one quality, which is sound alone and no other;
wind is proclaimed to have two qualities, namely sound and touch.
Sound, touch, and form are the three qualities of fire;
sound, touch, form, and taste are the four qualities of air.
Touch, sound, taste, form, and smell are the qualities of earth;
it is said that Brahmā’s origin occurs through the union of these combined elements.
All living beings, having gathered together, are born from portions of Brahmā.
And eighty-four hundred thousand species of living beings have indeed been proclaimed.
"By their nature they are happy beings, but through evil they partake of suffering;
by a mixture of both, they experience a mixture of results"—so it has been said by those who teach the Avadānas.
In India as well, it was likewise declared by the sages who advocate the doctrine of karma:
"There were seven hunters in the Daśārṇa forest, and deer on Mount Kāliñjara. (KDA 107)
The cakravāka birds on Śaradvīpa and the swans in Lake Mānasa were also born in Kurukṣetra as brahmins who had mastered the Vedas.
And it has been said by the Sage in the Laws of Manu:
"A Brāhmaṇa who lives by a wrong livelihood is indeed fallen. (KDA 109)
For one who has drunk the saliva of a *vṛṣalī*, who has been afflicted by her breath,
and who has slept with her— no atonement is found.
He who eats continuously for one month from the hand of a Śūdra woman shall remain a Śūdra while living, and after death he is reborn as such.
Having studied the four Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs according to the truth,
a Brāhmaṇa who accepts gifts from a Śūdra is born as a donkey.
For twelve births he is a donkey, for sixty births a pig, and for seventy births a dog; thus Manu has declared.
Thus it is also said in the Avadāna by the Buddha, the proponent of non-duality:
"A Brahmin who took what was not given became the lord of monkeys. (KDA 114)
There, with joy, he gave a *paṇa* coin to the Lord Buddha;
thereafter, having become a young man, that child indeed became a giver of dust.
By the fruit of that karma, he became King Sarvānanda;
there too, he joyfully offered alms-food to the Lord Buddha.
Through his devotion to Dīpaṃkara, that bodhisattva became a king;
having fulfilled all the perfections, he too shall become a Buddha.
Thus it was said in the Avadāna by the Jina, the proponent of non-duality;
therefore, one should understand that there is indeed no living soul (jīva), O Brāhmaṇa.
One is not a Brahmin merely by birth; rather, a twice-born becomes so through consecration.
If one were already a Brahmin by birth, the rule for consecration would be in vain.
For it has been stated in the *Smṛti*: "O twice-born one, one is not a Brahmin by birth or by dharma;
even a dog-cooker (*śvapaca*) becomes a twice-born man if he abides in the conduct refined by dharma."
For thus it has indeed been declared by Manu in the Laws of Manu: KDA_121.
The great sage named Kaṭhina was born from the interior of the fire-drill (araṇī);
he became a Brahmin through asceticism (tapas). Therefore, birth is not the cause [of being a Brahmin].
The great sage named Vyāsa was born from the womb of a fisherwoman;
through ascetic penance he became a brahmin. Therefore, birth is not the determining factor.
The great sage named Vasiṣṭha was born from the womb of Urvaśī;
he became a Brāhmaṇa through ascetic penance. Therefore, birth is not the cause [of one's status].
The great sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was born from the womb of a deer;
he became a Brahmin through asceticism. Therefore, birth is not the cause [of one's status].
The great sage Viśvāmitra was born from the womb of a Caṇḍālī;
he became a Brāhmaṇa through asceticism. Therefore, birth is not the cause [of one's status].
The great sage named Nārada was born from the womb of a grain of rice;
he became a Brahmin through asceticism. Therefore, birth is not the cause [of one's status].
In this way, all other sages as well became celibate Brahmins through austerity;
though born from the wombs of Brahmin women, they became true Brahmins by means of their ascetic practice.
Indeed, all human beings are Brāhmaṇas by virtue of their cultivation of dharma;
by the measure of their conduct in accordance with dharma, all men may become Brāhmaṇas.
All this is of a single color, having arisen from the creation of Brahmā;
it is only through the conceptual differentiation of the Dharma that the four castes have been devised.

All mortals are indeed born from a womb; all possess urine and excrement; and all have the same purpose regarding the functions of the senses. Therefore, O twice-born ones, [one is distinguished] by the qualities of virtuous conduct.
Even a Śūdra who is endowed with moral conduct and possessed of virtues may become a Brāhmaṇa;
whereas even a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of ritual action is inferior to a Śūdra.
Since there are indeed many types of castes distinguished by qualities, dharmas,
and conducts among all men born of Brahmā, what is the basis for their distinction?
Just as no distinction is perceived between gold and ashes,
so indeed there is no distinction whatsoever between a Brahmin and one of another caste.
Just as a distinction is perceived between light and darkness,
no such distinction exists between a Brāhmaṇa and one of another caste.
"O Brahmin, the Maruts did not arise from space, nor was Jātavedas born by piercing through the earth, as he is born from fire-sticks. (KDA 136)
Brahmins are born from a womb, and even Caṇḍālas are born from a womb;
what then is the distinguishing cause for superiority or for being a low-born person?
A Brahmin who has abandoned a corpse is also said to be loathsome and impure; so too are other castes and even those of mixed birth—what then is the distinction in this matter?
Just as there are characteristics such as the distinctness of the footprints of animals like lions,
what specific distinction exists among humans by way of the signs of bodily configuration?
Just as there is a distinction among birds such as swans and peacocks, there is no difference between humans based on the color of their faces or their voices. (KDA 140)
Just as there is a distinction in the bodily forms of worms and insects,
even so, among the various classes of humans, there is no characteristic of difference whatsoever.
Just as there is a distinction in the forms of leaves and so forth among trees and plants,
so too there is no characteristic of distinction in the physical form of human beings.
Just as there is no distinct difference in the specific forms of grasses, medicinal herbs, and crops,
so too among human beings there is no distinct configuration characterized by different marks.
Just as there are no specific distinctions of color or form among species of grain such as rice,
likewise there are no specific distinctions of color or form among human beings.
Just as there is a distinction of color and other qualities among flowers such as the jasmine and the kunda,
there is no such distinction of color, fragrance, and so forth among human beings.
Furthermore, the specific qualities of water-born flowers such as the lotus—
their color, shape, and fragrance— do not exist in the same way among human beings.
Just as there is a distinction between the qualities such as the taste of fruits like the mango,
there is no such distinction between the qualities of the flesh and bones of human beings.
Just as there is a distinction among the six classes of flavors based on their qualities, tastes, and so forth,
so too there is no such distinction among humans regarding the six sense faculties.
Just as there is a distinction of substance, color, and so forth among metals such as gold,
so too there is no distinction of shape or color among human beings.
Just as there is a distinction in the shape and color of precious gems such as diamonds,
there is no such distinction in the physical form of human bodies.

The distinctions such as equal flesh and so forth, as well as the six sense faculties being the same, show that there is no difference in any respect; why then is there a sense of distinctness among bodies?
Just as children, while playing on the great highway, gather heaps of dust and themselves assign names to them. (KDA 152)
"This is milk, this is meat, this is ghee, this is curd"—
yet, indeed, dust does not become food merely because of a child's words.
In the same way, Subhūti, the four castes are merely conceptualized;
even this application by means of the designation "a heap of dust" does not exist.
Not by the hair, not by the ear, not by the head, not by the eye;
not by the mouth, not by the nose, not by the neck, and not by the arm.
Neither with the chest, nor with the side, nor with the back or the belly;
nor with the thighs, nor with the shanks, nor even with the nails of the hands and feet.
Neither by voice, nor by complexion, nor by all [physical] parts,
nor by sexual characteristics, nor even by any single distinction is there any difference found among human beings.
Thus, there is no distinct mark of birth as there is in other cases;
I consider that nothing serves as a common cause that possesses a characteristic of differentiation.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others as well are conceptualized by mere designation; indeed, they are proclaimed to be nothing more than designations.
Just as there is no difference among fruits produced from a single tree,
so too, for those born of one [source], what characteristic of distinction could there be?
Indeed, the distinctions of birth arise from the practice of virtuous qualities;
for this entire system of four castes in the world originates from Manu.
By the very measure of its qualities and properties, a genus possesses no measure at all;
and so it is declared by the Buddhists, who are experts in the meaning of the Avadānas.
Those humans who are profoundly peaceful, endowed with the vows of truth and Dharma,
are pure Brahmins who dwell in the four sublime abodes.
Having renounced all possessions and dwelling in the forest hermitage,
those twice-born who always devote themselves to Brahman are indeed forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas).

Those twice-born householders who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), devoted to the six duties, and engaged in the performance of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) are indeed preceptors (*upādhyāya*).
Indifferent even toward their own bodies, having abandoned the objects of sensory experience,
subsisting on alms and established in their vows— those are the mendicants who proclaim the Brahman.
And those men who, having completely conquered the Māras, are unattached and firm-minded,
shine within the fields of merit— they are the true ascetics.

Those who have exhausted the ten unwholesome actions, who are devoted to the ten wholesome actions, whose speech is truthful, and who abide by their vows— those sages are the best of the twice-born. (KDA 168)
Those who have desisted from worldly activities, whose minds are fixed on the Dharma,
who are restrained in speech, those auspicious ones are sages who speak the truth.
And those who have conquered the collection of their senses, who are liberated from the prison of worldly existence,
who are free from "mine-ness" and free from egoism— they are indeed ascetics and practitioners of yoga.
And those wise men who, relying on a sacred mound, diligently observe their vows— they too are known as Sthaṇḍilas, O matted-haired ones.
And those heroes who have their limbs smeared with ashes, adorned with necklaces and ornaments,
are the Kāpālikas who practice the cemetery vow.
Those who, with concentrated minds, offer oblations of kindled sacrificial materials into the fire,
are the true Hotṛ priests and performers of sacrifice, the achievers of the goals of the Vedas and Dharma.
And those who, guarding the kṣatra, always protect the subjects,
whose conduct is devoted to the vow of protecting beings— those men are kṣatriyas and kings.
Those kings who, employing statesmanship, delight the people in matters of dharma and worldly affairs, are great heroes and the protectors of all dharmas.

And those who, for the sake of bringing about the welfare of sentient beings, cause the people to enter the Dharma by means of various beneficial activities— these indeed are Vaiśyas, the best among men.

Those Śūdras and likewise merchants who, devoid of vows and proper conduct, act solely for the sake of protecting their wealth and consider that purity comes through service— they are [the ones described].
And those men who plow the fields to produce rice and other grains—
those farmers sustain living beings with their grain.
Those who accomplish great tasks by means of collecting wealth and other goods,
being engaged in the work of trade, are merchants of great enterprise.
And those men who, having gathered caravans and come together at the mines of jewels,
acquire precious gems, are caravan leaders.
Likewise, those other men who practice the arts, sciences, and so forth are artisans;
and others as well, such as goldsmiths and the like, are also [artisans].
Even those men who are experts in the science of astrology, who calculate day and night,
and who understand the time of the end of the eon— they too are but calculators.
Having thoroughly understood the defects of the elements of the worlds, those who, as attendants,
administer medicine— they indeed are physicians and healers.

Having recognized the faults of elemental spirits, those humans who pacify those spirits through the performance of offerings and worship are also considered practitioners of the elements (bhautika). KDA_184 //
And likewise, whatever actions other sentient beings habitually perform,
by the influence of those very actions they proceed according to the nature of their rebirth.
Then those Mānavas who were cruel, merciless, harmful to living beings,
and whose conduct was characterized by fierce behavior, are known as Caṇḍālas.
Those who constantly worship Śiva, being devoted solely to devotion to Śiva,
are to be known as Śaivas, because they follow the dharma of Śiva.
Those men who constantly worship Viṣṇu, being devoted solely to devotion for Viṣṇu,
and who practice the religious duties of Viṣṇu— they too are Vaiṣṇavas.
Those men who indeed worship Brahmā, being solely devoted to the worship of Brahman,
and who practice the dharma of Brahman— they too are Brāhmaṇas.
Those men who worship Mahāraudra with minds devoted to Bhairava are known as Mahāraudras and Bhairavikas.
And those men who, following the family dharma, worship the goddess Māheśvarī,
upholding the vows of Māheśvarī— they too are [devotees of] Kālikā.
Those humans who always worship the Buddha and are devoted to the Buddha's Dharma are also Buddhists,
achievers of the state of perfect enlightenment.
Those humans who worship the Jina alone and are devoted to the Jaina Dharma are also Jains,
because they practice the Jaina Dharma.
And likewise, those other beings who follow the marks of ascetic vows—
all those young men as well— are describers of the practice of Dharma.
Whatever kind of action is performed, such will be the resulting birth;
for Prajāpati became devoid of distinction when he was in a state of unity.

whether one belongs to the Brahmin caste or another caste, there is no distinction whatsoever among them.
For superiority in this world is not justified by self-exaltation;

Those who travel through the sky fall because of eating meat;
having seen the downfall of the Brahmins, one should therefore avoid meats.
By what means one eats meats, by that very means one does not eat [them]. Furthermore,
by eating what is unfit to be eaten, a Brahmin becomes fallen.
A fallen brahmin likewise does not deserve the purificatory rites again;
therefore, without knowledge, one cannot truly be a brahmin by body alone.
For even among men who are Brahmins, one who possesses knowledge is worthy of honor; and when bodies are equal, where does any distinction lie? (KDA 218)
Therefore, by means of the measure of knowledge, there is no measure of the body;
just as a potter fashions vessels out of nothing but clay.
There is no difference in the clay, even in the vessels made from it;
rather, it is indeed designated by the names of the objects placed within them. (KDA 220)
Just as a vessel is identified by the substance placed within it,
so too is a person identified by their knowledge, virtues, qualities, and conduct.
A human being devoid of knowledge, dharma, virtues, and right conduct is a beast;
the differentiation of qualities proceeds from the distinction between knowledge (jñāna) and realized wisdom (vijñāna).
From the distinction of qualities, the distinction of phenomena arises;
from the distinction of phenomena, the distinction of actions subsequently proceeds.
From the differentiation of karma, a diversity of conduct likewise arises;
and through that specific conduct, the various distinctions of caste are brought forth.
In the aggregates and sense-bases produced from the great elements,
and in the bodies of all living beings which are equal [in this regard], what distinction can there be?
Indeed, human beings are distinguished by their knowledge and discernment;
because they are vessels for knowledge and discernment, even those of low birth are honored.
Because he lacks both knowledge (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*), even a human being is not worthy of worship;
such a person is like a beast in human form, and therefore worship is not for the physical form alone.
Even by means of knowledge, a twice-born man is not [a Brahmin] merely through the authority of ritual conduct;
for if it were by knowledge alone, then even a Śūdra would become a Brāhmaṇa, O Vipra.
There are also many others of low birth, such as fishermen and the like;
those who possess wisdom and are steadfast should indeed be considered Brāhmaṇas.
Therefore, one certainly does not become a Brahmin by mere knowledge alone;
nor is there any authority for knowledge based on the authority of ritual action and conduct. (KDA 230)
Even by means of action, a twice-born man is not [a Brahmin] solely on the basis of pure conduct;
for if it were by action alone that one becomes a twice-born, then indeed everyone would be a Brahmin. (KDA 231)
Indeed, there are many in the world who perform great sacrifices and other rites—kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras; why then are they not considered brahmins? (KDA 232)
Therefore, men certainly do not become Brahmins through action alone;
nor likewise do men become Brahmins through mere conduct alone.
If all were indeed Brahmins by virtue of their own conduct, then whoever possesses good conduct would surely be a Brahmin. KDA_234 //
There are many Śūdras endowed with pure conduct,
and there are even those of low birth who are most devoted to vows, fasts, and dharma.
They too would be Brahmins in this way if conduct were the authoritative criterion;
therefore, by conduct alone, humans are certainly not Brahmins.
Even by means of the Vedas, those supreme among men would not truly be Brahmins;
for if one were a Brahmin merely by the Vedas, then even a Rākṣasa would surely be twice-born.
Thus there was a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa who had mastered the Vedas;
indeed, all the Rākṣasas likewise followed the practices of the Vedas.
How could those [others] not be Brahmins? For if one becomes a twice-born (dvija) from the Veda, then surely they would not be Brahmins by the Veda alone.
By the standard of truth and dharma, this entire world is eternally one;
it is only by the heretics that this world has been conceived as consisting of four castes.
And thus it is postulated by the non-Buddhist outsiders for the sake of worldly understanding:
"Indeed, these four castes have arisen from the body of the Self-Existent One."
The Brāhmaṇa was born from the mouth; the Kṣatriya is recorded as having arisen from the two arms;
the Vaiśya originated from the thighs; and the Śūdra emerged from the feet.
If such a fault were indeed present in the teachings of those who praise [their own] doctrines,
then how could there be purity of doctrine through such acts as approaching those who should not be approached?
If the Brahmin was born from the mouth, where did the Brāhmaṇī originate?
Since the Brāhmaṇī was also born from the mouth, how indeed could she be both one’s sister and one’s wife?
And likewise, if those born as Kṣatriyas were produced from the arms alone,
then a Kṣatriya woman would indeed be the wife of a Kṣatriya and his own sister.
For a Vaiśya woman, likewise born from the thighs in this same manner, may become the wife of a Vaiśya; indeed, a Vaiśya woman is the sister of the Vaiśya class.
Just as a Śūdra is born from the feet [of Brahmā], so too is a Śūdrī produced;
indeed, a Śūdrī may become the wife of a Śūdra, for she is truly his sister.
It is not proper for a sister to be a wife; how, then, could that be dharma?
For by approaching one who should not be approached, only non-dharma (adharma) would arise.
Then it would be utterly contradictory if Brahmins were born from Brahmā;

And likewise in Bhārata, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira,

Who are those who are called brahmins, or what is the defining characteristic of a brahmin? O venerable one, I wish to know this; may you explain it to me.
Having heard this, the highly wise Vaiśampāyana respectfully replied:
"O son of Kuntī, listen as it is told by me."
Endowed with virtues such as patience, having laid aside the rod and being free from worldly desire, one does not harm any living beings; this is the first characteristic of a Brahmin.
When one never takes another's property, whether on the road or in the house, without it being given— that is the second characteristic of a Brahmin.
But he who, having abandoned his cruel nature, is free from the sense of "mine" and without possessions,

Indeed, the constant renunciation of sexual intercourse with women— whether they be gods, humans, or even those born of animal wombs— is the fourth characteristic of a brahmin.
Truth is purity, purity is cleanliness, purity is restraint of the senses;

For one whose mind is endowed with equanimity toward all worlds as if toward their own child, Brahman arises; therefore, move about endowed with that equanimity.
For this is the supreme dwelling of Brahmā, the means for attaining Brahmā; having understood it, act for the sake of the world's welfare as one who dwells in the sublime abodes.
Then, having completely conquered the afflictions and being composed in your own mind,

Even if one is engaged in meditative concentration and dhyāna, if the mind is not truly composed,

Having heard this description of the qualities of the Three Jewels, Subhūti,

therefore, out of compassion, quickly lead me and cause me to enter the monastery.
Having heard these words of Subhūti, the forest deity understood that his mind was thus rejoicing in the paths to awakening.
Then, having taken hold of the celibate Subhūti,

the Blessed One, most serene and adorned with the [major] marks.

Equanimity should also always be maintained toward sentient beings as if they were one's own child;

Having heard these noble teachings, Subhūti was filled with joy;
having utterly conquered the hosts of afflictions, he beheld the Buddha-dharma.

Having realized the fruit of stream-entry, he became a disciple of the Sage.

"O Protector, grant me the going-forth; establish me in the true Dharmas.

Addressed by the Jina with the word "Come," Subhūti— shaven-headed, carrying a bowl, and his body draped in a well-folded outer robe—

Having attained self-possession through the grace of the Sage, he applied himself and dwelt in meditative concentration;

Having realized that all of saṃsāra is struck by impermanence and that the course of worldly existence is fragmented, he abandoned all afflictions; thus self-restrained, he became an Arhat in person, possessed of great supernatural power.
Completely free from passion, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space and dwelling in the essence of wealth,
he shattered the shell of the egg of ignorance like a mountain and attained the supernormal powers and the analytical knowledges.

Because he was turned away from honors and gains, he became one who was to be worshipped, revered, and saluted by the gods, asuras, and humans, including Śakra; he was a practitioner of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra).
Then the venerable Subhūti, being self-possessed, reflected:
"From where have I passed away and come here? By what karma and to where?"
Then he saw five hundred births;
having been born in the womb of a nāga and passed away from there, I have now come here.
Because of my habitual practice of hatred, I became cruel and a destroyer of the world; for that very reason, I have encountered this great calamity.
Now, however, you should practice in such a way as to abandon this anger,
on account of which very cause people wander in the hells.
Therefore, I shall practice free from attachment and free from egoism;
for from attachment arises illusion, and within illusion arises delight.
Attachment arises toward sensual pleasure; in attachment, delusion increases.
The mind of one who is deluded is tormented by the frustration of his own desired ends.
When the mind is afflicted by injury, the fire of anger blazes forth;
ignited by the fire of anger, it consumes others as well. (Speyer:
it consumes both self and others.)
As long as one's own mind is inflamed by the fire of anger through the winds of the afflictions, what is the use of asceticism? It is useless and serves only as a cause for suffering.
The merit of well-practiced Dharma,
accomplished through means such as generosity and ethical discipline over thousands of eons, can be consumed in an instant by the fire of anger.
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying the fire of anger, one should exercise restraint over the senses and dwell in solitude within the seclusion of the forest retreat.
And when I was forcibly seized and devoured by Garuḍa,
I attained death upon seeing ascetics and offering them my approval.
For that very reason, having been born today into a family of the twice-born,
I shall become a celibate student after completely conquering all afflictions.
Even now, if I were to dwell here in this hermitage of the countryside in such a manner,
and if I were afflicted by some [obstacle], I would thus incur a fall.
Having thus resolved in his mind, the wise Subhūti, free from egoism and unattached, dwelt in a secluded forest retreat.
Dwelling there alone, endowed with the fourth dhyāna,
content with fruits, roots, and water, he rejoiced as a celibate practitioner.
Then, when he desired to wander even among the villages, regions, and districts for the sake of alms, KDA_344.
Then, having previously seen it, he observed the range [of his vision]:
"Alas! In all regions, people are devoid of virtue."
Arrogant, blinded by the delusion of pride, wicked, envious, and deceitful—
how shall I wander here from house to house for the sake of alms?
Some, upon merely seeing me as an ascetic, will corrupt their minds;
and for this reason, people wander even into miserable states of existence.
For thousands of millions of eons, they were not liberated from the miserable states;
therefore, I [dedicate this] toward all sentient beings, even down to the ants and termites.
Taking hold of a mind of compassion, one should dwell intent upon meditation,
so that the minds of all sentient beings may be thus gladdened;
by contemplating that very Dharma, the ascetic shall attain liberation.
Having thus girded himself with resolve in his mind, the highly intelligent Subhūti dwelt even in a secluded forest region, devoted to meditative concentration.
Then, at the end of three months, that Arhat, whose mind was set on enlightenment, reflected thus for the sake of benefiting the world: (KDA 351)
What enlightenment for the world can I achieve here while absorbed in meditation?
And for how long could I remain like a piece of wood or a stone, merely existing?
Meditation that serves merely to satisfy one's own mind is a means for achieving personal happiness;
yet even if such happiness is attained, what essence is there in it without the benefit of sentient beings? (KDA 353)
Rising from that meditative absorption for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
I shall display miraculous powers and establish the great multitude in perfect enlightenment.
Having thus resolved in his mind, the prosperous Subhūti displayed a miraculous feat for the sake of disciplining sentient beings.
There, five hundred families of the mighty Garuḍas, created by his supernatural power, spread out in every direction.
And seeing these Garuḍas, the nāgas were terrified;
bewildered and fleeing hither and thither, they went for refuge to Subhūti.
Then, having been comforted by Subhūti through his own power of supernatural faculties,
all the nāgas were completely rescued from the suparṇas.
Furthermore, for the sake of disciplining the Suparṇas, Subhūti,
by means of the power and majesty of his own supernatural faculties (ṛddhi), manifested a great nāga. (KDA 359)
By that [serpent] as well, five hundred families of Suparṇas were pursued by the nāga from all sides, here and there.
Chased by him, all the Garuḍas were seized with terror;
bewildered, they fled hither and thither and sought refuge with Subhūti.
In that very manner, Subhūti likewise comforted and well protected all those garuḍas by means of his own power of supernatural faculties.
Thus, having seen those miraculous powers of that sage, Subhūti, all the multitudes of people were filled with joyful wonder.
Blessed is this powerful bhikṣu, an Arhat who serves the Perfectly Awakened One,
by whom all these nāgas and even the garuḍas have been protected.
Thus, having seen that they were all filled with serene faith, the Arhat Subhūti taught them the Dharma of loving-kindness for the sake of discipline within the True Dharma.
Listen all to my words, O Nāgas and Garuḍas alike:
if you seek refuge in me, dwell with minds full of friendliness.
All those who are happy in this world are practitioners of loving-kindness;
all those who are suffering in this world are men of anger.
Therefore, let an effort be made with reverence to abandon anger;
for as long as anger remains in the mind, loving-kindness cannot be cultivated.
There is no evil equal to hatred, and no austerity equal to loving-kindness;
therefore, loving-kindness should always be cultivated with effort and constant respect.
When the dart of hatred remains fixed in the heart, the mind finds no tranquility, one does not enjoy the bliss of joy, and one attains neither sleep nor steadfastness.
Those who harbor hatred do not come to an end even if one were to kill them for the duration of one's life;
but he who destroys anger alone has destroyed all his enemies.
A living being, by means of the blazing fire of conceptual construction that consumes the oblation of anger, first burns himself; he may or may not burn others.
Old age is the ruin of those who possess beauty; anger is the darkness even for those who possess sight;
it is the bondage of virtue, wealth, and pleasure. Therefore, let anger be restrained.
Even while experiencing divine enjoyments in a palace adorned with jewels,
a man agitated by anger cannot find sleep even when he lies down to rest.
Even entire regions were consumed by the fires of curses uttered out of anger by sages and yogins who subsisted only on water, fruits, and roots. (KDA 375)
That which was the great, fierce, and pitiless son of Śaṅkara, by the fires of his gaze and through the power of his wrath, burned Kāma, the son of Brahmā.
When kings, having become hostile and fought with one another,
meet their death along with their people, that too is due to the state of anger.
When ignoble men, disregarding truth and righteousness, out of anger slay their friends and companions who act with affection and trust, [that is a great evil].
Even those virtuous and great-souled ones who practice the Dharma of proper conduct,
the wicked strike down in their very presence with the arrows of harsh speech out of anger.
Out of the power of their anger, they mercilessly kill even their own children, as well as their mothers who gave them birth or their nurses who protected them with affection.

Disregarding their gurus, the teachers of the true Dharma, and those who lead them onto the auspicious path,
sinful men, arrogant with anger, strike out in fearlessness.
Since even a father, when striking his own son or daughter— even a child—
without mercy, kills them, anger is therefore a great enemy.
Even brothers born of the same womb, when provoked to anger and their intentions divided, engage in conflict with great fury; therefore, anger is a great enemy.
Since even a wife who was lawfully wedded by oneself and who follows the dharma may be struck and abandoned by her husband out of anger, there is great danger from that.
And even a woman, disregarding family tradition, may likewise abandon her husband, her lord who acts with affection, out of anger.
Even those who are peaceful, self-controlled, steadfast, and dwellers in the four sublime abodes—
the wicked, filled with rage, strike them down in their very presence.
Peaceful in soul, a benefactor, a yogi, and a teacher of patience while dwelling in the forest—
even he was cut to pieces by the king himself with a sword in his wrath.
The Dānavas slay the gods, and the gods slay the Dānavas;
having engaged in mutual conflict, they crush one another, agitated by rage.
Having destroyed themselves by themselves through poison, weapons, fire, and the like, they too— all filled with rage— dwell in a terrible hell. (KDA 390)
Whosoever are of evil intent, cruel, and destroyers of their own and others' welfare—
all of them fall into the terrible hell because of their resorting to anger.
The world is divided by anger; by anger one is reviled;
indeed, a living being is harmed by anger; therefore, anger is the great enemy.
Out of sheer anger, Mahārudra severed the head of Brahmā;
by that very sin, Śiva became distracted in mind.
In that same way, out of anger, Rudra severed the head of Dakṣa, the son of Surajyeṣṭha and his own father-in-law;
indeed, because of that sinful deed, even Śiva became naked.
Through anger, righteousness is destroyed; through anger, it goes to ruin;
through anger, truth is abandoned; therefore, anger is the great enemy.
Whatever great evils and great fears of suffering there may be,
all those wicked things arise from a mind of anger.
No other enmity or greater sin exists than that arising from anger;
therefore, with concentrated minds, strive for the destruction of anger.
By him who has conquered anger— the adversary— through the virtuous Vajra of Wisdom,
all wicked enemies who inflict suffering have been conquered.
Even if he is a virtuous man, one who has no compassion in his heart and is consumed by the fire of anger is not trusted by people at all.
For one who is stained by anger, even if adorned with excellent virtues,
should not be served— even if he is wise— just like a tree entwined by a serpent.
Even if one is adorned with the practice of the true Dharma, such as generosity and ethical discipline,
if one is possessed by anger, one does not shine at all, just like a lake filled with snakes.
Even if he is knowledgeable in all sciences and arts, prosperous, and skilled in craftsmanship;
even if he is proficient in the use of missiles and mantras—if he is prone to anger, he must never be served.
One who is prone to anger is ridiculed by the world; one who is prone to anger is slain by people;
one who is prone to anger is abandoned by friends; one who is prone to anger is treated with contempt.
Anger, because it is contrary to the Dharma, brings about the destruction of the fourfold aim;
therefore, with concentrated minds, strive for the destruction of anger.
By anger the mind is split; one whose mind is split is scattered;
being scattered, one is afflicted by Māras; being afflicted, one falls into a lack of fortitude. (KDA 405)
Through lack of steadfastness one becomes deluded; being deluded, one falls under the sway of the wicked. By the instruction of evil friends, the person of base intellect wanders upon a wrong path.
One who has ascended the path but practices in a contrary manner,
through that contrary understanding, becomes a reviler of the noble ones.
Having rejected the true Dharma and so forth, and having destroyed images and the like—
by committing such a primary transgression, one incurs the five deeds of immediate retribution.
And from there he would go to the hells, such as Raurava and others, on all sides;
having gone from one hell to another hell, he would undergo great suffering.
Thus experiencing suffering, he shall dwell forever in the hells;
even the Jina would not be able to rescue him from those hells.
Know for certain that all the evils and sufferings which arise from misconduct originate indeed from a mind of anger.
The Jinas have declared that anger is the root of all transgressions,
whereas forbearance is the root of all virtues, from which happiness proceeds.
Thus, having completely conquered anger, one should always strive for patience;
maintaining a mind of loving-kindness, dwell at ease.
If one were to have compassion for others as one does for oneself, or as one does for one's own kin,
whose mind indeed would ever become inauspicious through an inclination toward unrighteousness?
Due to the absence of compassion, the world undergoes the utmost transformation,
through the fluctuations of mind, speech, and body, toward its own kin just as toward strangers.
One who seeks the Dharma should not abandon compassion, for it brings about the arising of desired fruits;
indeed, it gives birth to virtues just as a good rain produces crops.
A mind overcome by compassion does not become impetuous toward harming others; when it is pure, speech never becomes distorted, nor does the body.
Thus, for such a person, an increased delight in the welfare of others, accompanied by loving-kindness, generates qualities such as generosity and patience, which are followed by renown.

The compassionate person does not cause distress to others due to their tranquility; the compassionate one becomes trustworthy to all worlds, like a kinsman. Agitation born of fury does not prevail in a heart governed by compassion, for the fire of anger does not blaze in a mind cooled by the water of compassion.
In brief, the wise, through their steadfastness, perceive the Dharma as compassion. What virtue indeed is beloved by the virtuous that has not followed upon compassion?
Therefore, having brought compassion to its highest degree toward all people—regarding them as a son or as oneself—abiding always in true friendliness, you should manifest sympathetic joy. (KDA 419)
In the heart of the compassionate one, loving-kindness arises that accomplishes the true Dharma;
therefore, establishing compassion within the heart, let loving-kindness be extended toward the world.
A virtuous person who possesses loving-kindness is praised even by the gods;
they are always trusted by the good, by kinsmen, by relatives, and by all people.
In this world, a virtuous person endowed with loving-kindness shines even if devoid of other qualities;
one who possesses loving-kindness and noble intention is a kinsman to all people and to the entire world.
Possessing loving-kindness, he is beloved by the worlds; possessing loving-kindness, he is a well-wisher to the worlds;
possessing loving-kindness, he is a friend to the worlds; possessing loving-kindness, he is a companion to the worlds.
Wherever a person endowed with loving-kindness and glory goes,
there and everywhere he is honored just as if by his own kinsmen.
For the Buddha is the kinsman of the worlds, the leader and sovereign of the three realms;
even he, the Teacher, shines forth thus, ennobling the world with loving-kindness.
Whosoever are beings possessing great supernormal powers and compassionate toward all worlds,
they too are honored by the world of beings through the power of loving-kindness.
The Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who accomplish the equipment for enlightenment and abide for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, they too practice loving-kindness.
That a mother, though herself suffering, protects her infant son from the time he is in the womb through the application of affection— that too is due to the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
That a father, though not eating himself, protects his young son with happiness through the service of affection— that too is due to the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
And that the king himself, upholding the vow of a hero, protects his subjects while crushing all wicked people— that too is due to the power of his loving-kindness.
And when a wise teacher, demonstrating the meaning of the true Dharma to his disciples,
instructs them by awakening them like children, that too is due to the power of loving-kindness.
And that the heroes, standing in battle, endure their striking enemies and protect their own side— that too is due to the power of loving-kindness.
Having gone to the ocean, the caravan leader, acquiring jewels through great effort,
protects sentient beings by bestowing gifts, and that [protection] is due to the power of his loving-kindness (*maitrī*). (KDA 433)
And that a wife follows her deceased husband even at the cost of disregarding her own life— that too is due to the power of their friendship.
Out of affection, he also offers the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) with reverence even to his deceased ancestors,
repeatedly lamenting for them, and that [benefit] arises through the power of his loving-kindness (maitrī).
Even animals born of animal wombs, though cruel-minded,
protect their own offspring out of affection, and that is due to the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Even worms, insects, and cruel birds such as vultures protect their own kin out of affection; for that is indeed due to the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Even Caṇḍālas—who are pitiless, fierce, delighting in the injury of living beings, and wicked—protect their own kin; for that is indeed due to the power of loving-kindness.
That great beings give whatever object is requested by supplicants, even without regard for their own bodies, is indeed due to the power of loving-kindness.
In this way, other people as well, while providing for one another,
protect each other out of great affection and through the power of loving-kindness.

For loving-kindness is the mother of the worlds, the father, the teacher, the preceptor, the lord, the husband, the friend, the well-wisher, and the kinsman; therefore, let loving-kindness be cultivated.
Without loving-kindness, compassion does not arise even toward one's own child;
nor do sympathetic joy and equanimity. Therefore, one should cultivate loving-kindness.
These are called the divine abodes (brahmavihāra); they accomplish the state of perfect enlightenment, are the lords who sustain the three worlds, and are the protectors of all sentient beings.
Without these, ascetics do not shine, even after performing difficult austerities for thousands of millions of eons, despite possessing the great superknowledges.
For these are the supreme teachers who bestow the qualities of the true Dharma;
without them, those devoted to all the perfections do not attain success.
Know that all the various enjoyments of happiness, accomplished through merit in every way, indeed arise from the root of loving-kindness.
Therefore, having conquered anger with every effort even at the cost of your lives,
establish loving-kindness in your hearts and practice forbearance toward all living beings.
Then, through the power of the Dharma, you shall all rejoice; having enjoyed happiness for as long as you live, you will go to Sukhāvatī. (KDA 448)
Having heard these words of the ascetic, the nāgas and garuḍas abandoned their lingering resentment and became practitioners of loving-kindness.
Having seen this, those beings, filled with wonder and joy,
rejoiced in the Dharma and became practitioners of loving-kindness.
In this way, by that Subhūti, those nāgas and garuḍas were disciplined in the true path of Dharma through the instruction of the Dharma of loving-kindness.
Then the Blessed One, the Buddha, the all-seeing guide,
addressed the monks who were practicing within the realm of conventional truth.
"Behold, O monks, the celibate Subhūti,
by whom these garuḍas and nāgas have been disciplined in the true path of the Dharma."
Among my disciples, the monks who lead the holy life,
this son of good family, Subhūti, is the foremost of those who dwell in the state free from strife.
Thus, by that Lord of Sages,
Subhūti alone was designated as the foremost among all monks who dwell in the state free from conflict (*araṇā*).
Then all those monks, their minds agitated by doubt, questioned that Lord, the cutter of doubts, in this manner: KDA_456.
"Venerable sir, what deeds were performed by Subhūti,
on account of which you have declared him the eldest among those who dwell in the state free from conflict?"
Thus questioned by those monks, the Blessed One spoke as follows:
"Listen, all you monks, to that which was done by Subhūti."
Who else shall experience the karma performed by Subhūti?
Whatever karma has been performed by whomsoever, that very person experiences its result.
In the past, in a time long gone, during this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan was twenty times a thousand years; KDA_460.
And at that time, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa, the Leader,
perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, and a Jina.
The Teacher of gods and humans, the charioteer of men to be tamed,
the omniscient Blessed One, the Protector, the Lord of Sages endowed with the six superknowledges.
Residing at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park, the hermitage of the Jina, he dwelt there,
teaching the true Dharma to all sentient beings.
Within that very pure teaching, well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
he then became a great donor after having gone forth as a renunciant.
For ten thousand years he observed the vow of celibacy, and that best of those who know Brahman made this aspiration: KDA_465 //
By this merit, may I become a true disciple of the Buddha,
such as that one who was [ordained] by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the protector of beings.
"O young man, you have been prophesied as 'Uttara' for the sake of awakening;
O young man, this shall be when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years."
"You shall become Śākyamuni, the Great Buddha, the Omniscient One, the Leader of the World, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Blessed One, the Protector, and the Tathāgata."
And may I become the foremost disciple under his very teaching,
having attained the highest rank among those Arhats who dwell in meditative absorption.
By that very same karma, he has today entered my teaching and attained the preeminence among Arhats who dwell in the state of passionlessness (araṇā).
Furthermore, what were those very actions performed by him,
because of which he was reborn in the womb of a nāga?
Because their afflictions have not been abandoned, their faculties and minds are deranged;
[this applies] to monks who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as to those living the holy life (*brahmacārin*).
With this angry mind and harsh,
unsteady heart, having thoroughly corrupted his own thoughts, he has even rendered them impaired.
Having cried out with the words "O ever-poisonous serpent! regarding that which belongs to the Saṅgha, by that very transgression, he likewise [suffered] for five hundred births.
This man of great venom was born from the womb of a nāga;
yet, having again gone forth into homelessness there within the teaching of the Buddha, [he attained liberation].
Having always bestowed gifts and maintained the holy life,
he has now joyfully attained and realized the state of an Arhat.
"Indeed, I have designated him as the foremost among those who dwell in passionlessness.
Thus, O monks, you should understand this as the fruit of karma."
Whichever person has performed whatever action, that very person will certainly experience its fruit. For actions are not destroyed even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Having obtained the collection of conditions and the right time, [karmas] indeed bear fruit for embodied beings.
Karma is never exhausted by any means anywhere unless it has been experienced;
karma is not burned by fires, nor is it dried up by winds,
nor is it moistened by waters, nor does it perish even within the earths.
Furthermore, the course of actions is never otherwise for us:
white deeds always result in whiteness, and black deeds indeed result in blackness;
but mixed deeds certainly result in a mixture, to be experienced within the six realms of existence.
Therefore, having cast aside dark and mixed actions,
those who desire happiness should strive only for auspicious deeds.
"So be it," the monks replied; and those people who had been addressed, having drunk the nectar of the Buddha’s words, rejoiced with approval.
"Thus it is, O Great King; this was heard by me as spoken by my teacher.
Thinking thus, O King, you who desire the welfare of both yourself and others," [KDA 483]
Having diligently conquered the enemy of anger and being established in the dharma of patience,
cultivate loving-kindness toward all beings just as you would always toward your own children.
Having heard this well-spoken word of the true teacher Upagupta,
the king, together with his assembly, rejoiced, saying, "So be it."

Those who hear or cause others to hear this Dharma of the cultivation of loving-kindness—which removes all afflictions, is the conduct of Subhūti, and bestows happiness upon the three worlds—having gathered throngs of people:

those beings, possessing minds of loving-kindness, bestowing happiness upon the three worlds, and endowed with patience and gentleness, go to Sukhāvatī and there they honor the Dharma of the Sage Amitābha.
